channel.title: SARS-CoV-2: A History Run-Through
channel.description: A chronological walk through the SARS-CoV-2 literature, 2020 to the present — one landmark paper per episode, in the order it was published, with a focus on genomics.
channel.itunes:author: Nigel

item.title: Episode 5: Structural basis for the recognition of SARS-CoV-2 by full-length human ACE2 — Science, 4 March 2020
item.description:
Yan et al., "Structural basis for the recognition of SARS-CoV-2 by full-length human ACE2." Science, 4 March 2020. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb2762
The first atomic-level view of the receptor. In early March 2020, days before the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Renhong Yan, Qiang Zhou and colleagues at Westlake University solved two cryo-electron microscopy structures: full-length human ACE2 at 2.9 angstroms, and the SARS-CoV-2 receptor binding domain bound to that same full-length ACE2, also at 2.9 angstroms. To stabilise ACE2 — a single-transmembrane protein that is otherwise too floppy for high-resolution reconstruction — they co-expressed it with its known chaperone partner, the amino-acid transporter B0AT1, which contributes bulk and anchors the complex in the membrane. The structure revealed that full-length ACE2 is an obligate dimer locked together by a previously unseen neck domain, that the dimer can hinge between open and closed states, and that one ACE2 dimer can simultaneously accommodate two spike trimers — but only when each engaging RBD is in the up conformation Wrapp and McLellan had reported two weeks earlier. A residue-by-residue comparison with the equivalent SARS-CoV complex pinpoints specific changes — notably Lys417 gaining a salt bridge with ACE2 Asp30, and Phe486 enlarging a hydrophobic contact — that help explain the ten-to-twenty-fold tighter binding reported for the new virus's spike. This episode walks through the B0AT1 scaffolding trick, the cryo-EM pipeline, the open/closed dimer dynamics, the atomic-level map of the virus–receptor interface, and what the structure said in March 2020 about receptor engagement — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.

item.title: Episode 4: The proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2 — Nature Medicine, 17 March 2020
item.description:
Andersen et al., "The proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2." Nature Medicine, 17 March 2020. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-020-0820-9
The first origin-of-the-virus paper in a top journal. In mid-March 2020, less than a week after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Kristian Andersen, Andrew Rambaut, Ian Lipkin, Eddie Holmes and Robert Garry published a Perspective in Nature Medicine arguing from genomic data that SARS-CoV-2 was neither a purposefully engineered virus nor plausibly the product of cell-culture or animal passage in a lab. Their case rests on two features of the spike: a receptor binding domain whose high-affinity grip on human ACE2 uses a different residue solution than pre-pandemic computational models had predicted an engineered RBD would use, and a brand-new polybasic furin cleavage site at the S1/S2 junction with three predicted O-linked glycans around it, absent from every sampled bat or pangolin sarbecovirus. They lay out two natural scenarios — adaptation in an animal host before zoonotic transfer, or adaptation in humans after an initial cruder jump during a period of undetected transmission — and decline to pick between them given the data available at the time. This episode walks through the genomic comparison, the furin cleavage site and glycan argument, the recombination fingerprint from the pangolin receptor binding domain, and the specific logic the authors use to push the laboratory scenarios off the table — all from the standpoint of what was known in March 2020.

item.title: Episode 3: Cryo-EM structure of the 2019-nCoV spike in the prefusion conformation — Science, 19 February 2020
item.description:
Wrapp et al., "Cryo-EM structure of the 2019-nCoV spike in the prefusion conformation." Science, 19 February 2020. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb2507
The show leaves genomics for structural biology. In February 2020, Daniel Wrapp, Jason McLellan and colleagues at the University of Texas at Austin solved the first atomic-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structure of the SARS-CoV-2 spike ectodomain in its prefusion conformation, at 3.5 angstroms. The construct carried the two-proline stabilising mutations McLellan's group had previously worked out for RSV and other coronaviruses — the design that went on to become the antigen in essentially every spike-targeting COVID vaccine. The map showed the trimer predominantly in a one-up-two-down receptor-binding-domain arrangement, surface plasmon resonance put the spike-ACE2 equilibrium dissociation constant at about 15 nanomolar — roughly 10- to 20-fold tighter than SARS-CoV spike binds the same receptor — and three published SARS-CoV antibodies failed to bind the new receptor-binding domain. This episode walks through why the prefusion state is the vaccine target, how the 2P stabilisation works, how cryo-EM at this resolution is done, and what the up-versus-down RBD dynamic means for both receptor engagement and antibody recognition — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.

item.title: Episode 2: A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin — Nature, 3 February 2020
item.description:
Zhou et al., "A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin." Nature, 3 February 2020. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2012-7
The companion report to Episode 1. In February 2020, Peng Zhou, Xing-Lou Yang, Xian-Guang Wang, Zheng-Li Shi and colleagues at the Wuhan Institute of Virology recovered five full-length genomes of the new coronavirus from seven ICU patients in Wuhan, independently confirming the Wu et al. report. They then pulled a previously-sampled bat coronavirus, RaTG13, from a horseshoe bat in Yunnan out of their archive, sequenced it in full, and showed it was 96.2% identical to the new virus across the whole genome — the closest known relative. The paper is best remembered for the receptor-usage experiment that showed the new virus uses human ACE2 to enter cells, which set the target for essentially every COVID vaccine and monoclonal antibody that followed. This episode walks through the pan-coronavirus PCR screen, the metagenomic genome assembly, the RaTG13 phylogenetic placement, the spike receptor-binding motif comparison, and the HeLa-cell ACE2 transfection assay — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.

item.title: Episode 1: A new coronavirus associated with human respiratory disease in China — Nature, 3 February 2020
item.description:
Wu et al., "A new coronavirus associated with human respiratory disease in China." Nature, 3 February 2020. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2008-3
The first episode of SARS-CoV-2: A History Run-Through. In February 2020, Fan Wu, Yong-Zhen Zhang, Edward Holmes, and colleagues published one of the first two Nature reports characterizing the novel coronavirus behind the Wuhan pneumonia cluster. Using unbiased meta-transcriptomic sequencing on a single bronchoalveolar lavage sample, they recovered the complete 29,903-nucleotide genome of a previously unknown sarbecovirus — most closely related to a bat SARS-like coronavirus at the whole-genome level, and bearing a receptor binding domain that looked built to grip human ACE2. This episode walks through why meta-transcriptomic sequencing was the right methodological choice, how the phylogenetic placement and recombination analysis were done, and what the receptor binding domain comparison allowed the authors to predict about human transmission — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.
